newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Minor Metals - Japan traders buying cobalt.
newsitem.headline: Asian Minor Metals - Japan traders buying cobalt.

text.p: Japanese traders are buying cobalt on the spot market as they do not expect prices to fall further, and are likely to boost imports next month when metal firms start their new accounting year, traders said on Tuesday.

"Local end-users were sidelined when cobalt prices eased earlier this year. But they have now come back to the market, buying three to five tonnes per lot," a major Tokyo-based trade house official said. Cobalt is currently traded at around $23 to $24 per lb for higher grade Western material and about $22.5 for lower grade Russian cobalt, the traders said.
End-users are cutting their cobalt inventories ahead of their new accounting year which begins on October 1, they said.
"We expect accelerated buying from Japan next month," another trade house official said.

But Chinese demand for cobalt is slack due to a lack of available cash, a Chinese trader said. He was able to move small quantities -- 500 kg, one tonne, two tonnes -- at a time. "But it is difficult to find people who have the cash to buy," he said.

Chinese magnesium was being offered at well below prevailing world levels, trading sources in Hong Kong and China said, citing prices of $2,200 a tonne, compared with $2,550 for Western and CIS material.
They said the competitive pricing was keeping Chinese magnesium sellers active, although concerns about quality would continue to dampen enthusiasm for the Chinese product.
Industry experts believe China's magnesium supply capacity is between 60,000 and 80,000 tonnes a year, and its domestic consumption about 10,000 tonnes.

Between 200,000 and 300,000 tonnes of magnesium oxide are believed to have been smuggled out of China in 1995, which led authorities to crack down on ports through which the metal, used in the production of aluminium and aluminium alloys, was likely to have been moved.
Japanese magnesium traders said they have covered their near-term requirements through long-term contracts, and have no immediate plans to buy in the spot market.
"Some Chinese traders are offering us cheaper magnesium than world markets, but there's no active buying interest on our side," a magnesium trader at a major trade house said.
The only other bright spot in China's minor metals market was ferro-molybdenum, traders in Beijing and Hong Kong said.
Chinese sellers were asking between $10 and $12 per kg, the traders said, reporting a jump of up to $4 per kg in the past couple of months.
Demand was coming mostly from steel makers in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan, one trader said, citing a little interest from Europe and the United States.

Germanium oxide remained of greater interest, a Chinese trader said, though prices had dropped in the past two or three weeks by $100 per tonne to $1,130. This compares with the latest London indicated price for germanium at $1,700 a tonne.
